beats.narration: A customer email arrives. Their Sprout reports soil moisture of minus four thousand percent, and then waters their cactus until it floats.
Minus four thousand percent? How is that even possible?
Integer overflow, somewhere. And there is a second complaint: Sprouts in hot rooms read the soil as wetter than it is.
Math on a microcontroller is not math on a calculator. Numbers have fixed sizes, some operations are slow, and there may be no floating point hardware at all.
Today, the team learns to compute with confidence.
Not all arithmetic costs the same. On a small processor, the difference between the fastest and slowest operations can be a hundredfold.
Additions and shifts are basically free. Multiplication is cheap on most modern microcontrollers. Division is slower.

beats.narration: Floats have numerical traps too. They cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly, so comparing two floats for exact equality is risky.

beats.narration: And adding a tiny number to a huge one can do nothing at all, because the tiny one falls below the huge one's precision.

beats.narration: First, the minus four thousand percent. Ada finds this line.
A sixteen bit signed integer holds values up to thirty-two thousand seven hundred sixty-seven. A raw reading of four thousand times one hundred is four hundred thousand.
It overflows, wraps around to a negative number, and the division makes nonsense of it.
Widen the type before the multiplication, not after. Casting the result of an overflowed calculation is too late; the damage is done.
Saturating is clever. Instead of wrapping from the maximum to a negative number, clamp at the maximum.

items: Know the range of every variable
Widen before multiplying
Multiply before dividing, to keep precision
Watch for signed overflow: it is undefined
Saturate instead of wrapping when it matters

beats.narration: A moisture reading stuck at one hundred percent is wrong, but much less wrong than minus four thousand.

beats.narration: Sensor readings are noisy. The obvious fix is averaging. But there are several kinds of averages, with very different costs.
A simple moving average keeps the last N readings and averages them. Clear, but it needs memory for N readings.
A trick: keep a running sum, add the newest reading and subtract the oldest, instead of re-adding all N every time.
An exponential moving average needs no buffer at all. Each new reading nudges the average a fraction of the way toward it.

visual.title: Exponential moving average, integer only
lines: // new = old + (sample - old) / 8, with 4 fractional bits

beats.narration: Choose the fraction as one over a power of two, and the division becomes a shift.

visual.title: Exponential moving average, integer only
lines: // new = old + (sample - old) / 8, with 4 fractional bits

beats.narration: Notice the extra fractional bits. Without them, small differences round away to zero, and the average gets stuck short of the true value.

visual.title: Exponential moving average, integer only
lines: // new = old + (sample - old) / 8, with 4 fractional bits

beats.narration: Keeping four extra bits of precision avoids that.

visual.title: Exponential moving average, integer only
lines: // new = old + (sample - old) / 8, with 4 fractional bits

beats.narration: Which one should we use?

visual.title: Exponential moving average, integer only
lines: // new = old + (sample - old) / 8, with 4 fractional bits

beats.narration: For the soil, the exponential average. One variable, a shift, and an add.

visual.title: Exponential moving average, integer only
lines: // new = old + (sample - old) / 8, with 4 fractional bits

beats.narration: And maybe a median of three first, to throw out single wild spikes before they reach the average.

beats.narration: The biggest speedups usually come not from faster arithmetic, but from smarter algorithms. Sprout's schedule search is a good example.
The old code checks every schedule entry, one by one. With ten entries, who cares. With a thousand history entries, it matters.

beats.narration: Keeping the list sorted lets us use binary search: halve the list at each step.

visual.title: Operations to search a schedule list

visual.title: Operations to search a schedule list

beats.narration: Can it be computed incrementally as data arrives, instead of all at once?

beats.narration: Like the running sum. Instead of summing everything again, we just adjust.

beats.narration: The temperature compensation uses an exponential function, computed in software floats. Ada asks: how accurate does it actually need to be?
The soil sensor itself is only accurate to a few percent. Computing the correction to ten decimal places is pointless.
A simpler formula that is accurate to a tenth of a percent is plenty.
Many smooth functions can be approximated by polynomials over a limited range. A few multiplications and additions replace an expensive library call.
Taylor series are one way to find such polynomials; curve fitting on real data is another.
Writing the polynomial in nested form, called Horner's method, minimizes the number of multiplications. Three coefficients, two multiplies, two adds.

visual.title: Polynomial in Horner form
lines: // correction = a + t*(b + t*(c)), integer coefficients scaled by 1024

beats.narration: And check the error across the whole range. An approximation that is perfect at room temperature and wildly off at forty degrees is a bug waiting for summer.

visual.title: Polynomial in Horner form
lines: // correction = a + t*(b + t*(c)), integer coefficients scaled by 1024

beats.narration: Division is slow, but dividing by a constant is a special case. The compiler, or you, can replace it with a multiplication and a shift.
Fifty-two thousand four hundred twenty-nine divided by two to the nineteenth is very close to one tenth.

visual.title: Division as multiply and shift
lines: // x / 10 for 16-bit x, without a divide instruction

beats.narration: Multiplying by it and shifting right gives the same answer as dividing by ten, for every sixteen bit input.

visual.title: Division as multiply and shift

beats.narration: Compilers already do this automatically when the divisor is a constant they can see.

beats.narration: Sometimes the fastest computation is no computation. A lookup table stores precomputed answers, and the code simply reads them.
Our probe's response is not a straight line. So instead of a formula, we store calibration points measured with real soil, and interpolate between neighbors.
Five points and a little interpolation replace a complicated curve. More points mean more accuracy and more memory. The table lives in flash, costing no RAM.

visual.title: Linear interpolation between table points
lines: int i = find_segment(raw);                    // which pair of points

beats.narration: And when we change probe suppliers, we measure a new table. No code changes.

beats.narration: For the remaining math, Ada switches to fixed point: storing fractional numbers as integers with an agreed scale.
In this format, the top eight bits hold the whole part and the bottom eight hold the fraction.
Three point two five is stored as eight hundred thirty-two, which is three point two five times two hundred fifty-six.
Addition works directly. Multiplication needs a correction: multiply two scaled numbers and the scale doubles, so you shift the result back down. All of it uses fast integer instructions.
The price is range and precision. Choose the scale for your data: enough fractional bits for the precision you need, enough whole bits that values never overflow.
The temperature compensation now runs in integers. Twenty times faster, and Gerald cannot tell the difference.
Write the scale into the names. A variable called moisture q eight or temperature centi degrees tells every reader what one unit means.
Mixing up scales is the classic fixed-point bug, and naming prevents most of it.
Many teams pick one or two standard formats for the whole codebase, rather than inventing a new scale for every variable. Fewer formats, fewer conversion mistakes.
Investors keep asking about AI. Can Sprout have AI?
Actually, a little bit, yes. Small neural networks can run on microcontrollers, using fixed-point math much like what we just did.
A model trained on a big computer can be shrunk, converted to eight bit integers, and run on the device.
It could learn each plant's drying pattern and water just before it gets thirsty.
But be honest about it. A model needs data, testing, and memory. If a simple rule does the job, the simple rule wins.
Machine learning is a tool, not a marketing requirement.
I heard marketing requirement.
To recap. Learn which operations are cheap on your chip, and avoid software floats in hot loops. Size your integers, widen before multiplying, and clamp instead of wrapping.
